title: A Father Passes On Wisdom
overview: A parent urges his children to hold on to wisdom as he once learned it from his own father, contrasting a path that grows brighter with one that ends in darkness.

parts.label: A call to listen (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: The speaker addresses "sons" in the plural, which may mean his own children or students he treats like family. He presents his teaching as solid and worth keeping, not just rules handed down.

parts.label: What grandfather taught (vv. 3-9)
parts.note: The speaker remembers being a young, much loved child and repeats his own father's words, showing wisdom handed down through three generations; tradition links this to Solomon quoting David. Wisdom is pictured as a woman to love and embrace, who in return protects and honors you, like a victory wreath placed on your head.

parts.label: The first step (v. 7)
parts.note: The Hebrew here is compact and a little puzzling, but the point seems to be that wisdom starts with simply deciding to go after it. It is worth more than anything else you could spend your resources on.

parts.label: A clear, open road (vv. 10-13)
parts.note: Following this teaching is pictured as walking a straight path with room to move, where even running will not trip you. The instruction is something to grip tightly, because it is described as your very life.

parts.label: The other road (vv. 14-19)
parts.note: People who do harm are pictured as so driven they cannot sleep until they hurt someone, as if wrongdoing and violence were their daily food and drink. Their way is like deep darkness where you trip without knowing why, while the good person's way is like dawn growing into full daylight.

parts.label: Guard your heart (vv. 20-27)
parts.note: In Hebrew thinking the "heart" means the inner self, including thoughts, choices and desires, so guarding it means watching what shapes you from the inside. The father then moves through mouth, eyes and feet, asking for honest speech, a steady focus and careful steps that do not wander toward harm.

think: What lessons from the people who raised you do you still find yourself repeating, and which ones would you choose to pass on?
